subject: Medicine
summary: Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) is an ascending infection of the upper genital tract, most often from sexually transmitted organisms. Early recognition and broad‑spectrum antibiotics prevent infertility and ectopic pregnancy.

sections.p: PID is inflammation of the uterus, tubes, or ovaries caused by bacterial invasion. Diagnosis relies on clinical criteria plus laboratory support.
b: History of sexual activity, pain, fever, abnormal discharge

t.b: Detect cervical motion tenderness, adnexal tenderness; positive findings support PID

t.a: NAAT for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae
t.b: Identifies common pathogens; a positive result confirms etiology and guides therapy
Leukocytosis suggests infection; normal counts do not exclude PID
Elevated values support inflammation but are nonspecific

sections.p: Severity is graded by the CDC 2015 criteria: mild, moderate, severe, or fulminant. Fulminant PID requires hospitalization and IV antibiotics.
b: Mild: low fever, mild pain; moderate: higher fever, moderate pain; severe: high fever, significant pain; fulminant: septic shock, organ failure

sections.p: The leading causes are sexually transmitted infections, especially chlamydia and gonorrhea. Other bacteria and local factors also contribute.

t.b: HIV infection increases PID risk and severity
May alter flora and mask symptoms

sections.p: Patients report lower abdominal pain, fever, and abnormal vaginal discharge. Cervical motion tenderness is a key sign.

t.b: Central pelvic pain suggests tubo‑ovarian involvement; flank pain may indicate pyosalpinx

sections.p: Laboratory and imaging confirm diagnosis and rule out mimics.

t.b: Detects tubo‑ovarian abscess, free fluid, or ovarian cysts; normal in early PID
Rule out ectopic pregnancy if pregnancy test positive

sections.p: Complications can be life‑threatening and include sepsis, abscess, infertility, and ectopic pregnancy.
Treat empirically with broad‑spectrum antibiotics covering gonorrhea, chlamydia, and anaerobes. Adjust therapy based on culture and local resistance.
b: IV therapy for severe cases: ceftriaxone + metronidazole + azithromycin
Monitor for treatment failure or complications

sections.p: Ensure treatment completion, test‑treat‑treat (partner notification), and counsel on barrier contraception.

t.b: Rule out pregnancy before prescribing certain antibiotics

sections.p: Differential diagnoses include ectopic pregnancy, ovarian torsion, appendicitis, and urinary tract infection.
Normal CBC or ultrasound does not exclude PID; low-grade fever may be missed.
b: Normal leukocyte count in early PID
Pregnancy test false negative if early pregnancy

whenToSeekHelp: Evidence of ectopic pregnancy (positive pregnancy test with abdominal pain)

faq.q: Can PID happen without sexual activity?
faq.a: Rarely; non‑sexual routes include post‑operative infection or contaminated tampons, but sexual transmission is the main route.
Yes, with appropriate antibiotics; however, scarring can lead to infertility or ectopic pregnancy.

faq.q: Do I need to see a doctor if I have mild pain?
faq.a: Any pelvic pain with abnormal discharge or fever warrants evaluation to rule out PID.

exam: Explain the CDC 2015 severity criteria for PID and how they guide treatment decisions.
Describe the rationale for empiric antibiotic choices in PID, including coverage of anaerobes and resistance patterns.
Outline the steps you would take to manage a patient with suspected PID who is pregnant.
